data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The nocturnal UHI is an emergent geometric radiative-trapping effect: the single mechanism that explains both its existence and its cross-city variation is the sky view factor. Urban street canyons with tall buildings have a reduced view of the cold sky, so longwave radiation emitted by warm surfaces is partially absorbed and re-emitted by building walls rather than escaping to space, dramatically slowing the nocturnal cooling rate. Cities with deeper canyons (taller buildings relative to street width) have lower sky view factors, trap more longwave radiation, and exhibit a larger nocturnal UHI. The effect is absent or reversed during the day, making it a purely nocturnal phenomenon.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If cloud cover is present, the sky emits as a warm blackbody and the sky view factor advantage disappears entirely.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If urban materials have very low thermal mass (e.g., light timber construction), there is little stored heat to trap and the geometric effect alone may be insufficient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If wind speed is high, turbulent mixing bypasses the radiative trapping mechanism.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"On a clear, calm night, the dominant cooling mechanism for any surface is longwave radiative loss to the cold sky. The rate of this loss is proportional to the sky view factor, the fraction of the sky hemisphere visible from the surface. In the countryside, the sky view factor approaches 1.0, so rural surfaces radiate efficiently to space and cool rapidly. In a city, buildings reduce the sky view factor to as low as 0.3 in deep street canyons. Longwave radiation emitted by the road surface is intercepted by building walls, which absorb and re-emit it, effectively trapping heat within the canyon. This radiative trapping slows the urban cooling rate independently of thermal mass or anthropogenic heat. The single mechanism explaining cross-city variation is therefore the sky view factor: it is a geometric property that depends on building height and street width, and cities with denser, taller construction have lower sky view factors and larger nocturnal temperature gaps.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
